# CHAPTER XVIII

FREE FIGHT (1869-1870)

The old New Englander was apt to be a solitary animal, but the young New Englander was sometimes human. Adams discovered the charm of Washington spring. The Potomac and its tributaries squandered beauty. Rock Creek was as wild as the Rocky Mountains. The brooding heat of the profligate vegetation; the cool charm of the running water; the terrific splendor of the June thunder-gust in the deep and solitary woods, were all sensual, animal, elemental. No European spring had shown him the same intermixture of delicate grace and passionate depravity that marked the Maryland May. He loved it too much, as though it were Greek and half human.

In spite of the fatal deception about Grant's political character, his first winter in Washington had so much amused him that he had not a thought of change. Henry was in a savage humor on the subject of Boston. Fifteen or twenty years afterwards, Clarence King used to amuse him by mourning over the narrow escape that nature had made in attaining perfection. Except for two mistakes, the earth would have been a success. One of these errors was the inclination of the ecliptic; the other was the differentiation of the sexes. Adams, in his splenetic temper, held that both these unnecessary evils had wreaked their worst on Boston. Of course he was in the wrong. The thinness was in himself, not in Boston; but this is a story of education, and Adams was struggling to shape himself to his time.

Before he got back to Quincy, the effects of President Grant's character showed themselves. They were startling—astounding—terrifying. Jay Gould's attempt to corner gold in September, 1869, was a scandal at which Charles and Henry Adams jumped like salmon at a fly. Charles took the railway history; Henry took the so-called Gold Conspiracy. The Congressional Investigation furnished the material. The trail always faded and died out at the point where any member of the Administration became visible. Adams himself feared finding out too much. He found out too much already, when he saw that Jay Gould had actually succeeded in stretching his net over Grant's closest surroundings. That Grant should have fallen, within six months, into such a morass rendered the outlook for the next four years—probably eight—possibly twelve—mysterious, or frankly opaque, to a young man who had hitched his wagon, as Emerson told him, to the star of reform. The worst scandals of the eighteenth century were relatively harmless by the side of this, which smirched executive, judiciary, banks, corporate systems, professions, and people, all the great active forces of society, in one dirty cesspool of vulgar corruption.

His four most powerful friends in the Administration had matched themselves, two and two, and were fighting in pairs to a finish, with foreign affairs and the judiciary as prizes. The Senate Chamber became a scene of irritated egotism that passed ridicule. Senators quarrelled with each other and picked quarrels with the Executive and threw every Department into confusion. Society laughed a vacant and meaningless derision over its own failure. Nothing remained for a young man without position or power except to laugh too.

Yet the spectacle was no laughing matter to him. Society is immoral and immortal; it can afford to commit any kind of folly, and indulge in any sort of vice; it cannot be killed, and the fragments that survive can always laugh at the dead; but a young man has only one chance, and brief time to seize it. Any one in power above him can extinguish the chance.

The political dilemma was as clear in 1870 as it was likely to be in 1970. The system of 1789 had broken down, and with it the eighteenth-century fabric of *a priori*, or moral, principles. Politicians had tacitly given it up. Grant's administration marked the avowal. Nine-tenths of men's political energies must henceforth be wasted on expedients to piece out—to patch—or, in vulgar language, to tinker—the political machine as often as it broke down. The moral law had expired—like the Constitution.

All this was excessively amusing. Adams never had been so busy, so interested, so much in the thick of the crowd. When spring came, he took to the woods, which were best of all, for after the first of April, what Maurice de Guérin called "the vast maternity" of nature showed charms more voluptuous than the vast paternity of the United States Senate. Senators were less ornamental than the dogwood or even the judas-tree. The Administration drove him, and thousands of other young men, into active enmity, not only to Grant, but to the system or want of system, which took possession of the President. Every hope or thought which had brought Adams to Washington proved to be absurd. No one wanted him; no one wanted any of his friends in reform; the blackmailer alone was the normal product of politics as of business.
